---
title: "Beyond the periodic table"
description: "Use R to check a language-model system. Learn where evaluation, workflows, LangChain, LangGraph and LangSmith fit."
---

The table lists separate text tasks. A system can join several tasks.
For example, it can find a document, write an answer, and update a record.
You must check the whole system as well as each task.

This section starts with one worked lesson:
[Compare two system versions in R](evaluating-systems.qmd).
You will check invented test results. You will not call a model.
You do not need an account, an API key, or Python for this lesson.

## Start with the right question

An **evaluation** checks whether a system meets a stated requirement.
A higher average score is not enough. A system can answer more questions
correctly and still skip a required check before it changes a record.

The worked lesson asks you to decide whether to **release** version B.
Release means allowing people to use a version.
You will compare it with version A on the same cases.
You will keep missing results in the total and check the rule used to grade
each result.

## What to read first

You need basic R. You should know data frames and the pipe, `|>`.
You will run the supplied code and read its results.
The lesson explains the evaluation terms when you need them.

## Where the tools fit

The tool descriptions below were checked on 21 October 2026.
They describe documented features. The worked lesson does not run these tools
or test a connection between them.

LangChain gives developers model and tool interfaces.
It also supports agent loops. An **agent loop** lets a model choose a tool,
read its result, and choose a next step.
Its official framework examples use Python or JavaScript/TypeScript.

LangGraph controls a workflow through explicit state and steps.
**State** is the information kept between steps.
A graph names the steps and the routes between them.
It can support loops, pause for a person, and resume later.
It does not require LangChain.
The reviewed documentation does not list an official R version of LangGraph.

LangSmith is a separate platform for traces, datasets, and evaluations.
A **trace** records the steps taken during a run.
An **SDK** is a set of code tools for a service.
The reviewed SDK list includes Python, JavaScript/TypeScript, Go, and Java.
It does not list R.
That does not prove that R cannot use its APIs.
An R connection through web requests or another runtime needs a separate test.
No such connection is tested here.

R also has native tools.
The ellmer package supports model calls, tool use, and outputs with named fields.
The vitals package organizes evaluation cases, solvers, scorers, and logs.
A **solver** produces a result. A **scorer** assigns a score.
These tools do not prove that R can save and resume workflows like LangGraph.

::: {.callout-warning}
## A local score can still need a network call

In vitals, `generate()` makes model requests, and `$eval()` solves and scores.
A scorer written in R does not make the solver network-free.
The documented default uses the same model to solve and grade unless changed.
A separate judge model also needs checks against independent human review.
:::

## Choose a workflow only when you need it

A fixed sequence, such as extract, check, and report, can be one R function.
Use that simple form when it meets the need.

A different process may pause for a person, keep its state, and resume later.
A graph runtime can help with that process.
Before you claim that it recovers after a crash, test a real restart.
A diagram, saved chat messages, or a checkpoint kept only in memory cannot
prove that behavior.

An optional later lesson can compare these designs.
This section does not yet provide a Python lab or an R-to-LangSmith connection.
